utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could while I'm on my feet, Mr. President, raise two other issues, the first having to do with the contested documents. We are in the process of providing a spreadsheet along the lines indicated by the Presiding Judge in the middle of last week. We hope to have that available by Thursday of this week, but we will certainly have it available by Friday of this week. I should also indicate that as far as we are able to ascertain, the only missing translations relate to the war logs or war diaries and several of the videotapes. It appears to the Prosecution that some of the material indicated on the legal officer's memo as being missing in fact is not missing from the copies of the binders that we have. So there certainly might be some instances where individual sets of the binders may be missing one or more documents, but in fact the Prosecution -- or other sets of those binders are complete. We are endeavouring to ensure that all the parties, as well as the Trial Chamber, obviously, have copies of all the documents, and we believe that there could be some administrative reasons due to the large volume of material that was photocopied in which some of the binders may not be as complete as they should be. So we are working on that. I should also, however, indicate that the war -- the diaries of the witness ZP who testified, certainly those diaries will not be available at any time in the near future due to the large volume of that material. Of course, those are not material that the Prosecution intends to tender into evidence but is simply being made available to the Chamber and the Defence for purposes of determining whether the witness may or may not need to be re-called as a Court witness. That's pretty much where we stand with respect to the contested documents and missing documents to those materials. I will, of course, continue to work with our case manager and the Trial Chamber's legal officer to identify any remaining gaps in that material in order to make it available to the Trial Chamber as quickly as possible, but we do expect to have the war logs or war diaries and the final video transcripts available by the end of this week, if not the middle of the week. And finally, Mr. President, I have one remaining issue that I would like to call to the Trial Chamber's attention: As Your Honours are aware, last week I was in Sarajevo interviewing some witnesses. One of those witnesses will be available, as I said, either Wednesday or perhaps Tuesday if that would be more convenient. Both of these witnesses relate to the Trial Chamber's oral order that we produce a witness who is capable of testifying as to technical issues surrounding orders. The witness for this week was formerly the communications officer of the 3rd Corps. His testimony will go to part of what the Trial Chamber has asked us to provide. The second witness was the Chief of Staff during part of the time period of the 3rd Corps. This witness as of right now does not possess a valid Bosnian-Herzegovinian passport. We are working with the Bosnian officials in order to expedite the issuance of such a passport. This witness is also listed on the filing that we filed in early June as being an individual that the Prosecution anticipated could have authenticated a large number of the documents that are on the contested exhibit list. During the course of the interview with this witness, he was shown three documents that the Prosecution submits has his signature on them. The documents obviously were photocopies. The witness, however, during the course of the interview indicated to us in the presence of the Defence during the videotaped interview that the signatures on the documents were "a good copy of his signature but in fact were not his actual signature." This raises several very important issues, Mr. President, and this is precisely why I felt that it was necessary to raise this with the Trial Chamber. Obviously the Prosecution as well as the Defence and the Trial Chamber are seeking here to ascertain the truth. We are now in a position where a witness that we anticipate calling could very well testify that some of the documents contained in the archives of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 3rd Corps may not be authentic documents. For this reason, Mr. President, the Prosecution will seek an adjournment as soon as the currently scheduled witnesses have testified in order that we may submit a number of documents to a forensic handwriting specialist to ascertain whether in fact these documents do support the Prosecution theory that the witness in question actually signed them. At the same time and in order to be as thorough and complete as possible and in light of what the Prosecution has previously indicated to the Trial Chamber, we believe it is important particularly at this point in time that those documents which purportedly bear the signature of the two accused also be submitted for forensic analysis. As I speak, one of our analysts is determining the precise number of documents that these three individuals signed - in the Prosecution's submission - that being the witness, the Chief of Staff witness that I spoke with last week, as well as the two accused. Once we have the total number of such documents, the Dutch forensic laboratory, which is the one that we primarily deal with, would be in a position to tell us approximately how long it might take them to review these documents. I understand, Mr. President, that this is a difficult situation, but in light of the fact that this witness has indicated that he did not sign these documents although he acknowledged that it appeared to him to be a, again, good copy of his signature, is extremely troubling to the Prosecution. But in our discharging of our duties in terms of seeking the truth, we believe that the best course is to ask for this adjournment and use the time during that adjournment to ascertain, if possible, whether these documents were signed by the individuals that the Prosecution believes they were signed by. I have not had a chance to discuss this with the Defence, because a decision was just taken shortly before this session. So I do not expect them to be in a position to respond. But our position at this point in time would be that we are not in a position to call the Chief of Staff as a witness until the issue of authenticity of the documents can be examined via forensic methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We would propose, in terms of an initial request concerning this adjournment, that we would again hear the witnesses, the two witnesses scheduled for this week; we then adjourn until immediately after the August recess, at which point in time we will be in a better position to know precisely whether or not the forensic expert has completed his report or at that time would be in a position to indicate when that report might be finished. And again, we are in the process of compiling those figures right now. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We just have the Criminal Procedure Code and the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, the Defence acquiesced to the request of the Trial Chamber because we feel it is indeed important that we have as an exhibit copies of the Criminal Procedure Code as well as of the Criminal Code that was in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. So the Defence is tendering the Criminal Procedure Code in English and the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina - also the English translation - copies of which have been provided to the Trial Chamber and the registry, and we are tendering them into evidence as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Two exhibit numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Criminal Procedure Code will be 337; and the Criminal Code, 338.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So we'll now have the technical break. It is ten to 4.00, and we will resume at twenty past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Registrar who has something to tell us about a number that has been given.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, document DH328 has been marked for identification, and the last two numbers, 337, that is, also have an English translation, and they will be entered as 377/E and 377/E for the English version of this document [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would kindly ask the usher to fetch the witness. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor for any documents which you might wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Not to tender documents, Mr. President, but simply, as promised, I would give you the numbers of the three documents that I showed the Chief of Staff last week, and I thought I would take that moment while the witness is entering the courtroom to do so. These documents are contested exhibit numbers 162, contested exhibit number 327, and contested exhibit number 573. It is the last document, number 573, that the witness basically indicated that he would not have signed such a document. Again, he was shown a number of other documents as well, but those are the three documents that the Prosecution asserted bore his signature. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber what my learned friend has said is quite correct. The only thing I would like to mention is that when he said he would not have signed such a document is -- what he meant was this was a political document and that's why he wouldn't sign it. Your Honours, if you wish to take a look at this document, you have to know why the witness said he would not have signed this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. First of all, can you hear the translation of my words into a language that you can understand? Can you just say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clearly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called as a Prosecution witness. I am going to ask you to take a solemn declaration. But before that, I would like you to give us your name and your date of birth, as well as the place where you were born.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My full name is Peter Desmond Hackshaw. My date of birth is the 8th of November, 1960. And I was born in New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your nationality or citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A New Zealander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And what is your current professional position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an investigator and acting team leader of investigation team 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international tribunal as an investigator or is this the first time you have been called to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please read the text of the solemn declaration shown to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, who are going to be putting questions to you, I would like to provide you with some information as regards your testimony here. You will first answer questions put to you by the Prosecution within the scope of their examination-in-chief. These will be followed by the questions put to you by the Defence counsel, who are going to lead their cross-examination. The main objective of the latter is to verify your credibility, and also they might want to ask you questions about the general context of their case. After that, the three Judges, who are sitting in front of you, can ask you questions. They can do that at any moment. The Judges prefer to wait until the very end because sometimes the Judges' questions will already have been answered by you in replying to the questions put to you by the Prosecution or the Defence. After that, the Prosecution and the Defence will have the right to re-examine, and these questions may be followed by additional Judges' questions. And after that both parties will have the right to put additional questions arising from the Judges' questions. Your testimony will take place today and tomorrow, but since you are a member of this institution, you will not have a problem staying here one day longer. You have just entered a solemn declaration and promised that you would tell the truth. That means that you will be telling the truth. And I have to remind every witness that if -- a false testimony may be subject to a heavy penalty or imprisonment. The second thing that I would like to mention, although it does not apply to you, is that in case a witness might incriminate himself in replying to any question, the Trial Chamber may grant such a witness a certain immunity. The questions may sometimes be complicated. If that is the case, you may always ask the party putting it to you to rephrase the question so as to enable you to answer it properly. So this was just general information as to how your testimony is going to take place. If you have any problems at any point, please ask the Judges to assist you. I don't know who is it going to be who will be leading the examination-in-chief, Mr. Mundis or Mrs. Benjamin. It seems that this is going to be Mrs. Benjamin. Mrs. Benjamin, you have the floor for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Hackshaw, could you state for the Trial Chamber for how long have you been employed with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Five and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For how long have you -- in what capacity were you employed?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: I started off as an investigator, and then about a year and a half ago I was asked to take the role of the acting team leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So firstly, state for the Trial Chamber your role as team leader, acting team leader.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: My role is to supervise, oversee the other investigators on my particular team as well as coordinate the activities of language staff that assist our team and the analytical support staff that are available to our team.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, was this role specific to any particular team?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. It's specific to investigation team 9, which is the team that is responsible for the investigation of those crimes alleged to have been committed by Bosnian perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And specifically, is team 9 attached to any particular case?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: A number of cases; obviously, the case against the accused Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura is one of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us now your duties as an investigator, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Principally they are to gather evidence, facts, testimony and documents that may be used to prove or disprove the matters under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, as an investigator, you -- your role begins from the instructions of a particular individual on the team; am I right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Obviously it depends on what point the investigation is at. Generally, pre the indictment stage we take particularly legal direction from trial attorneys who are also attached to that particular project. Obviously once it reaches the indictment phase, there is the senior trial attorney appointed to the case, if one is not already attached to the case, and we then take direction from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, could you walk the Trial Chamber through the case of investigations from the commencement of your instructions to the completion of your task. Tell us how it begins, from the time you receive instructions until they are completed.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Sure. In the particular case of -- against the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura, during 1999 the team conducted a research project trying to identify crimes throughout Bosnia that may merit further investigation, and as a consequence of that, the crimes in Central Bosnia that are alleged to be committed by members of the ABiH and the Mujahedin were identified as an appropriate project. The --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you for a while. You indicated that the team conducted a research project. Could you tell us how you went about doing this, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Principally we researched data, documents, that were contained within the ICTY OTP holdings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And when the research was completed? Could you move on to the next step.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: What we then had to do was to formulate an investigation proposal which we put to the senior management of the OTP, and at which point they approved it as an investigation. And from that point on, we commenced the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, what did this investigation proposal contain?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: It contained various allegations of criminal wrongdoing that we had identified and that we continued to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did the proposal in itself state how you were going to approach the investigations?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: To a certain degree, yes, investigation proposals do. Obviously there's always a need for flexibility in any investigation because things develop and -- you know, you can't necessarily guarantee what the outcome will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So we submitted an investigation proposal. And once the proposal was admitted, where do we go from there?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Then we formulate, I suppose, strategies about how things will be done. And in the case of the investigation into the ABiH and Mujahedin activity in Central Bosnia, it was decided that certain members of the team would investigate the crime-base or the alleged crime-base incidents further, while other investigators would look at the command and control aspects of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, how did you physically do this investigation? Did it warrant you staying at the ICTY, going on to the field? How did you conduct the investigations?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Both. It requires continued research into -- and analysis of our own holdings, as well as preparing and executing missions, the purpose of which is to gather evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, let us look at the latter part, the missions. Could you tell us how the missions were conducted.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Certainly. Generally we would have an objective -- or always we would have an objective that we hoped to achieve. For example, in the case of collecting crime-base testimony, an investigator would look at a particular crime; they would then endeavour to identify a number of witnesses that could give testimony about those events, and then the investigator would be required to write a mission plan, which outlines the objectives that he or she hopes to achieve, the persons that they intend to interview, the time frame involved, the expense involved, safety and security aspects involved. They would then give this proposal through the chain of command to obtain formal approval to be allowed to make that mission possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So we have executed the proposal and we're on our mission.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you give us a broad view of what transpires on the mission.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: This is where we travel into the field and you do your job, whether it be locating your witnesses and interviewing them, recording a statement, or whether it be looking through documents that are housed at a particular archive.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Let's take, for instance, the taking of statements. What is the purpose in mind when you take the statements, and how do you achieve the statements -- taking of the statements from the potential witness?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Basically, in the case of -- where you're interviewing somebody who has -- who doesn't speak English, the statements are recorded in English, they're typewritten, and done so through the use of an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, when you -- when you have a witness or potential witness that you are taking a statement from, what is -- how do you -- do you have a particular way that you take the statement? Is there a particular format?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, there is. The OTP has a witness-statement templates that used to record the details. It's -- basically it starts with a cover page where the witness details are recorded, and then you go into the body of the statement where the facts or information are recorded. It is then read back to a witness, and the witness -- in a language they understand and if there are any alterations to be made, those alterations are made. And then the witness is asked if they are happy with the statement to sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the instance when the witness may have referred to documents, how do you deal with recovering the documents?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Generally, where there are a number of documents either that perhaps we've taken down with us into the field that we want the witness to look at or where they provide documents in support of their statement, the most common practice is for those statements to be annexed to the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, what happens when the statement is taken and the mission is completed and you return to the ICTY? Can you explain to us the procedure that takes place there.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Certainly. When we return to the OTP the statement and any documents which are annexed to it or any audio-visual material that we've been given is submitted to the Evidence Unit. What we do is we enter the statement electronically into a -- or a reference to that statement into our electronic database that -- historically, that physical computer entry gets -- creates what used to be called an IF, or an indexing information form. And that indexing information form, along with the statement, gets - and any attachments to it - get submitted to the Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We have discovered sometimes that a witness may say, "I submitted X document," and this is not annexed to the witness statement. Could you tell us what happens in situations like that. What is the cause?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: The cause could be because it's a miscellaneous document which is not related to the specifics in the statement. If that's the case, the document or a piece of evidence should be entered into the index information form, should be given an index information form of its own, so as it's effectively recoverable by way of electronic search.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you assist us in the instance where a potential witness, when he eventually comes to court, says to us, or in the proofing, "I never said X." Could you explain to us what transpires during the taking of the statements.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, the investigator would take the statement through -- with the assistance of an interpreter. It then gets read back to the interpreter in a language that they understand. And then they are asked to sign it, to show that they accept that it's true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But these statements are never tape recorded, are they?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Not -- no, the policy is that witness statements should be typewritten. There undoubtedly are situations where material has been audio-recorded. Certainly if anybody is a potential suspect, then audio and/or video recording is the normal practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about the issue of protective measures? Do the witnesses or the potential witnesses indicate to you at the time of the taking of statements of a request for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes they do. And we had -- within our own team, we had witness information forms that we endeavoured to maintain for most witnesses which were supposed to clearly reflect any concerns they may have. Of course, frequently material is obtained from a witness and there's quite some passage of time that goes between them finally coming here to give testimony, if required, and obviously we have to re-check whether those protective measures are still in place at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But as an investigator with the OTP, if a witness requests or indicates to you that that witness received -- needs protective measures, certainly wouldn't the witness have to provide certain grounds to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, the witness would. I mean, we -- we would expect, although many, many of our witnesses have concerns, we expect it to be -- or them to be able to justify actual reasons for that concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And how do the investigators of the OTP go about verifying these concerns?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: If you're uncomfortable accepting what the witness has to say, then you would have to perhaps interview other persons, speak to the local authorities, review documents which may support what they've said. There are any number of means of obtaining verification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, sometime early in June of 2004 did you conduct one of these particular missions with respect to this case, Hadzihasanovic and Kubura?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I visited -- I was asked to visit the offices of the prosecution service in both Zenica and Travnik to look for any investigations or reports of crimes that had been referred through the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So you said you went to Zenica and Travnik. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I'd like you to walk us through Zenica mission first, please. Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Prior to going on this mission, one of the -- my colleagues that was involved had contacted both the prosecutor at the Zenica court and the -- sorry, at the prosecution service and the -- one of the prosecutors at the Travnik office of the prosecution service and asked them to provide all case files referred through the district military prosecution office for the period of 1993 and the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What was the purpose or the objective of this particular mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: The objective was to find what files had been referred through the district military prosecutor, as the information that I'd been provided with indicated that all military prosecutions or all reports of criminal activity or alleged criminal activity, the one point that all that information was supposed to go through was through the office of the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you go on this mission alone?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was accompanied by investigator Michael Koehler who is also on my team, and one of the leadership team analysts, Alasdair Macleod.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So could you step by step relate for the Trial Chamber concisely what the mission entailed; what you did, how you acquired what you acquired, if you acquired anything.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. We went to the Zenica -- the office of the prosecution service in Zenica, where they had collated the files that we had asked for, that is, all case files that they held that had been referred through the district military prosecution service. They had also compiled a number of case files that had been referred through the higher public prosecutor in Zenica, and we physically went through each of those files, the purpose being to try and see whether there was any investigation requests or reports that related to the crimes alleged against the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And were you looking at any particular area, or were you looking at all the crimes in general that's in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: We were looking at the -- specifically, we were looking for allegations which mirrored those within our indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you perused the records, as you indicated to us. And could you tell us a little bit about the system, how it was organised, what you found.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. In respect of the files that had been forwarded through the district military prosecution, there were actual case files of matters which had been finalised, which had been rejected, and which had been stayed. And there was a similar number of cases that had been referred through the higher public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Was there a register in place?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. They had registers, and they -- registers were prefixed with letters. And by that I mean the registers were used to show the receipt of any such file or report. Those that -- those case files that had known perpetrators were prefixed with the letters KT. Those files where the perpetrators were unknown were prefixed with the letters KTN. And there was a third register, which from our assessment of it looked like miscellaneous incoming correspondence, which was prefixed -- each item was prefixed with the letters "KTA."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. For example, let's say, for instance, we were looking at Dusina, for example. How would you go about looking at Dusina?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Initially, we endeavoured to review all the physical case files that were present, and there was only -- the only case files that were actually present were KT files, namely those that had known or named perpetrators. And through the use of an interpreter, they went individually through every single file that was made available to us, and we recorded brief details about each case file that was presented. Sorry, one thing I meant to mention is that at the Zenica office of the prosecution service they maintained separate registers for -- the higher public-prosecution service had a separate register in which they recorded all KT -- one for KT, one for KTN -- and the military prosecution service had maintained separate registers for KT and KTN cases, the difference in the main being that the military prosecution service related to -- or it appeared from our review that the military prosecution service related to matter where is military personnel were involved and the matters that were referred through the higher public prosecutors in the main were where civilian personnel were involved. However, we did come across cases where, in the higher public prosecution register, where civilian and military personnel were accused of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And how did you relate it to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Initially what we did was we went through the military prosecution files KT, which were the -- which were physically present, and we recorded short details of each one, and then we went -- sorry, and then we went -- sorry. Certain members were doing certain -- different piles. There were basically files that were given to us in a number of piles. And because of the short time that we had and the volume of materials, we just simply reviewed those files that had gone through the higher public prosecutor, namely the civilian -- or the alleged civilian perpetrator files.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, did you -- but how did you proceed to come to an analysis as to whether or not you found the file or you didn't find the file? Did you cross-match? How did you do this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yeah, we did. We basically found towards the end of the period that there were files missing, and obviously that's a serious flaw in the whole exercise. So what we tried to do was we tried to check the registers. Now, the registers are where each particular case is supposed to be logged upon receipt and then given its number. Once it became obvious that there were actual case files missing, we then had to go to the registers and try and record or review them, each individual entry, to see whether it related to anything in our indictment. Now, obviously with the volume of files that had been referred through either the district military prosecutor or the higher public prosecutor, it was -- we chose to focus on serious crimes against the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, what was the reason given for missing files?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: In relation to the KT --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And this is Zenica we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: In relation to the files -- the case files at Zenica, it was explained to us that certain files were considered open or case files were considered open and that they had been, once the district military prosecution office ceased to exist, they had been referred out to the municipal courts in -- wherever the crime was alleged to have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you have told us that you physically searched through each register. Now, in your search, did you find anything in relation to the offences mentioned in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: In relation to serious crimes against the person, for example murder or manslaughter or aggravated robbery, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about the -- under the KTN category, which is the unknown perpetrators? Were you able to come across anything related to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: What we had to do, because there were no case files to review, we selected the serious crimes against the person, and in most cases victim details were recorded in the register and we recorded those victim details. And then when we came back to The Hague we physically attempted to cross-reference the victims from the initial report to those that featured in our indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would I be correct if I said the analysis was basically the same for Travnik?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. We worked almost in reverse at Travnik, because when we arrived, they made it clear to us that there were certain case files missing. So as a consequence -- and because of even more serious time constraints at Travnik, we chose to look only at the registers in the first instance, and we tried to isolate those crimes that were serious crimes against the person, and then we tried to cross-reference. We then tried to find the case files that they referred to. And if they weren't present, we recorded the victim details from the register.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did any of the files you found in Travnik correspond to the offences you were looking for in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you told us on several occasions that you recorded and you made a record. How did you record this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: We recorded it simply in our notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And each member on the team recorded each person's task - am I correct - in different notebooks?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. For example, at the Zenica prosecution service, I had a pile of KT files that were finalised or in a binder that said they were finalised. So I recorded those details.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So if the Trial Chamber wishes to go into detail as to what you would have accomplished on the mission, would it be in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if I were to show you the notebook, would you be able to verify that that is the said notebook?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: I certainly would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may the witness be shown the notebook, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That's -- this is the notebook that I maintained throughout this three-day exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us, if there's some sort of order that you followed in the notebook, if you put it in different categories. How was the notebook compiled?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: First of all, it related --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have received these notes. I would just like to see exactly physically what the notebook looks like in order to be able to compare the notebook with what we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the notebook to the accused as well, please. We would like to have a look as well. You may proceed. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have looked at the notebook. I would like to remark that the numbers on the notebook and on the photocopy are not the same. My learned friend has already explained that. However, I would like my learned friend to tell us exactly what number we're dealing with when she's referring to the notebook. Otherwise, we will not be able to follow the examination-in-chief. It's very difficult for us to find the hour and the minutes, so if my learned friend could tell us exactly what pages she's dealing with, and if she could also tell us exactly what is the purpose of the question that she's putting and the notebook that she's showing to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Benjamin, why are you showing the witness the notebook? And secondly, could you please make sure to mention the number, because it seems that the numbers in the notebook do not correspond to the numbers in the photocopy. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my friend jumped ahead of me. But the purpose of actually wanting to put or intending to put the notebook in evidence is for the Trial Chamber to be able to see the way in which the documents were recorded and what was recorded, because certainly in the interest of time, I don't think we're going to be going through each item in the notebook; hence the reason. There is also, as my friend would see, three bundled he received. So far we have done the first one which is 0357-7025, which is his notebook. Have you seen it? Do you have it? Do you have it? Okay. And that is the sample that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, the Prosecution intends to show the witness the notebook because it wishes to tender the notebook into evidence. There are some other documents which I don't have, but maybe you will be able to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It is true that we have not discussed that in any detail. I didn't know that this will be tendered into evidence, but the witness is here and he will give us his conclusions before the Trial Chamber. However, the documents should be translated into the language that the accused can understand. And in addition to that, a motion should have been made for the changes in the list of evidence. That's the basic procedure. I didn't know that. I knew that this witness would come to testify. Last week I asked for this document because I knew that the document was mentioned, but not for a single moment did I think that it would be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, the Defence says that the document that you have in your hands and that is in English has not been given to the accused because it hasn't been translated, and this is a problem, obviously. The Defence counsel should be able to discuss any document with the accused in order to provide for the useful cross-examination. Since they have not been able to discuss the document with their clients because the document is not in B/C/S, there has been a problem which they have just mentioned. What is your reaction? How are you going to respond to this intervention?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the intention of the Prosecution was not for the document to be entered with respect to the content, but to the form and the way in which -- the procedure which was followed by the investigator. And I did indicate to my friend when he asked me for the notes on the document that we would be happy to present it for him so that they can see what transpired. As they went, they recorded. If the Defence has a problem with the procedure, then certainly we can -- we have no problem in withdrawing the notebook. But the only intention was to show the Court the system that is followed, really. It was just for -- not for substance, just for form. But if they have a problem with it, we can withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Bourgon, apparently you have been informed of the Prosecution's intention to tender this document into evidence, not the document itself because it has any particular value, but just to show the way an investigator works.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is possible that they -- that we have discussed that, but -- and I have received the document, but we have not discussed it in any detail. What I can tell you is that we have received a statement. I was in Sarajevo. We discussed this with my learned friend in Sarajevo. I asked why the statement wasn't signed. Then we spoke about that with our learned friends in The Hague, and we did not have any objections to this being shown in order to speed up the procedure. However, if my learned friend wants to talk about the procedure that was used, I believe that it is sufficient to have the witness here. The witness may be asked questions, and then the witness will be able to explain what procedure he applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, what's your response to this? Maybe you can ask the witness a question without actually tendering this notebook into evidence. The witness is here, and he is maybe best suited to tell us how he proceeded. And the Trial Chamber obviously will want to ask some questions because if we're talking about an investigator, then obviously this investigator will be able to clarify some matters for us. I know that he is an investigator, but I don't know what is he by profession, what are his professional qualifications. Maybe as an investigator he also could be an IT expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think, having walked the witness through the procedure that they undertook in relation to this specific mission and in relation to missions generally, the notebook was being tendered into evidence or attempted to be tendered into evidence to support or to corroborate what he actually just said. If my friends on the other side feels that, you know, it shouldn't be there, we don't have a problem. We've already laid the foundation as to how he did his work, how the mission was done, and he -- all he basically said is that he recorded each thing. Nothing in that notebook is of any value to us anyway. So we -- the Prosecution wishes to withdraw the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I think the Court was quite right in guiding us. I think we omitted in letting the Court know your professional qualifications. So maybe before we go on to the other aspect, could you please state for the Court your professional qualifications. We got how long you worked here but we didn't get your professional qualifications.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Prior to joining the transcribe, Your Honours, I spent 15 years in the New Zealand police, during which time I obtained my detective rank, and subsequently got promoted from being a detective to a sergeant and then back into the role of a detective sergeant within the criminal investigation branch.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Perhaps for the benefit of the Trial Chamber you can tell us what are the requirements when applying for the position of investigator at the ICTY. What professional qualifications are required?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Generally, in the majority of cases you're expected to have a police and law-enforcement background, with a strong previous background in serious-crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And we concluded what takes place on a specific mission, as you just indicated. Now, on your missions to crime-base areas or to the area where the conflict has arisen, did any time in your investigations would you have to pay visits to archives, courts, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the course of this investigation and others that are being conducted by our team or have been conducted by our team, we have visited a number of archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the mission was conducted relating -- in relation to archives specifically, and if any particular archive.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously the first phase of any such operation is to get permission to actually visit a particular archive. Once that permission has been granted, you would try and obtain as many persons to assist you as possible, and certainly, archive searches are not restricted to simply investigators. We rely on military analysts, leadership, research personnel, and obviously language support staff. We would -- depending on the objective of going to any archive, we would prior to going endeavour to make some sort of checklist which would give those that are perhaps not familiar with the case that we were relying on some broad outline of the type of material that we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And how was this exercise conducted physically?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: The actual search itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Well, generally, you simply visit the premises where material is stored, and with your interpreter you will try and gain an overview, or somebody would realistically try and gain an overview. For example, if I went to the ABiH military archive, common sense would say that if I'm investigating crimes in Central Bosnia, then I would focus more on the files that related to the 3rd Corps of the ABiH than I would to other corps, because that's their particular area of responsibility. And then we would -- you would physically start searching the binders that any such material is housed in, trying to gain an overview as quickly as possible in situ of what the binder contained or what the case file contained. Because time and resources are always a significant factor in any such search, you would -- if time allowed, you would try and photocopy as much of the material as you could so as it can be reviewed back in The Hague with more care, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How do you determine which document you seize from the archive?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Well, like I mentioned, if I was going down -- if I was organising a mission in relation to the alleged illegal activity of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, if I was looking for documents in -- that reflected any aspect of that, I would organise for a checklist to be made up of important places, dates, personalities, so as that those that didn't have as much understanding of the case had some mechanism in place to confidently at least review material.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You personally, in your dealings with the document, let's say from the ABiH archives. Do you remove original documents? Do you remove copies?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: In the case of the search we actually conducted at the ABiH archive, we were only given permission to photocopy material.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What of the civilian archives? Have you had conduct of investigating civilian archives in relation to this trial?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. We reviewed material that was housed in the Presidency archive, the Bosnian Presidency archive. There have been searches were also conducted at the headquarters of the 7th -- what was the old 7th Muslim Brigade - I understand it's now the 7th Mechanised Brigade - based in Zenica. We've conducted -- not me personally, but other members attached to the team -- have conducted a review of material at the archives of the Party of Democratic Action, or the SDA. There's been some review and searches through the military -- the ABiH military security archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you your observations on these archives, what would you say to the Trial Chamber with respect to your observations and the operations of these archives?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: It's fair to say that they vary considerably in how they are maintained, and they vary considerably in the volume of material that's housed within them. That's my observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When the investigation is completed and the mission is completed, when you return to The Hague, what is your role in respect to the continuance of the -- following the documents with respect to the trial stage? What is your role?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: We -- you need to -- the investigator needs to ensure the documentation is brought back, and depending on the quantity of material that's seized from a particular archive, you need to make sure that it's -- the security is -- of the transportation of that document or quantity of documents is maintained. For -- yeah -- then it's got to be submitted into the Evidence Unit. Now, in the case of the search that was conducted at the former ABiH archive, the volume of material was such that we actually sent somebody from the Evidence Unit down and they -- while we were searching on a nightly basis, the person from the Evidence Unit was down in -- at the Sarajevo field office where the documents were being kept and they were physically starting their evidence-stamping procedure, just to try and improve the whole processing of it once we got it back to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With respect to the crime-base witnesses, how did you proceed with the investigations in the field with respect to the crime-base witnesses? What was the criteria for choosing these witnesses? How did you go about this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: We would receive information about potential witnesses from a number of sources. Sometimes it was through previous witnesses that we'd already spoken to who nominated further witnesses who could help us. Sometimes it was through searches of our internal database where, if they'd been interviewed by other organisations and we'd been provided with a copy of their statement, we would go and revisit them. Sometimes it was through material that came to our attention by way of open source; open-source material, media articles. Sometimes, in the case of international witnesses, it was through -- again, through data that we already held or through other witnesses that we'd already interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And finally, when the statements are taken -- and correct me if I'm wrong -- I believe most of them are taken in Bosnia, in particular to this case. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: The bulk of what I would term "crime-base witnesses" were interviewed in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, when is the translation done? Because most of these witnesses are not English-speaking witnesses. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So could you explain to the Trial Chamber when the translation is done, how it's done, and when does the witness sign this document in his own language.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Generally, the witness doesn't sign a statement in -- that's been translated into his own language. What happens is the statement is brought back to The Hague, the statement is submitted to the Evidence Unit, and under the old indexing information form, which was the electronic form we generate for each document or statement that we bring back for each piece of evidence, there used to be a facility that was an electronic translation tab where you would request a translation of the statement which was recorded in English into a language -- into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So at the field office in Sarajevo, what does the witness sign?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: The witness signs -- in the majority of cases, the witness signs the English copy of the statement, which has been read back to them in a language -- in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a break, as is customary, and we shall continue at five to 6.00. After that, we will work until the end to have day, and I suppose the Judges will have quite a lot of questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hackshaw.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think we arrived at this Tribunal almost at the same time, and I know we've seen each other, but we've never had the opportunity of working together. For the benefit of the record, please let me introduce my team and I. I'm accompanied today by Mrs. Edina Residovic and by my colleague Mr. Alexis Demirdjian. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and together we represent General Hadzihasanovic. I have, of course, a few questions for you, and I think I can finish at least for my part today, which will leave the questions from the Judges -- from the Bench tomorrow. I'd like to begin by confirming a few of the details that you have given in response to questions that were put to you by my colleague from the Prosecution. I'd like to begin first by the fact that one thing was mentioned during your examination-in-chief, and that is that we have received from the Prosecution a statement which is in English and which is entitled "Declaration of Peter Desmond Hackshaw." That is yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it that this declaration is a declaration that you made yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You are the drafter of this declaration.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I just ask this question because the statement itself is not signed. But you acknowledge that this is your statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it also that since you did make this statement - and I think we've had it now for about a week - that you did not make any modifications to the statement that was disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And no additions were made to the same statement.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on by confirming that you have a background as a police investigator and that the matter of investigation itself is nothing new to you. You have a lots of experience in this field. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In fact, you've been working for a number of years before joining the ICTY as an investigator.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And today you are the team leader in, I guess, an acting capacity of team number 9, and you've been in this position for 18 months.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I'm the acting team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As far as the Tribunal goes, you have been at the Tribunal now for five and a half years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which I take it means that you have been involved in a number of investigations over and above the investigations related to this case.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I don't know and I would like you to confirm is whether you were always a member of team number 9 ever since you joined the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And beyond some deployments during 1999 in Macedonia, Albania and Kosovo, my entire working life at the Tribunal has been on team 9 projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And team 9, as you mention, is the team which is dedicated to crimes allegedly committed by Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct. It's the team that investigates crimes allegedly committed by Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: By Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Bosniaks includes also -- Bosniaks could be Croats from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you work on both sides, and not only specifically on crimes committed by Bosnian Muslims on the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's fair to say that it's crimes committed by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would hate the record to reflect that I thought the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina consisted solely of Muslims. That's -- that would be misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's a very, very -- I appreciate the answer, and I appreciate, of course, the difference between the two. So for you it's crimes allegedly committed by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, either against the two common enemies at the time, which is either the Serbs, but of course the Army of Republika Srpska, or the Croats, or the Army of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There could also be other possibilities.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your capacity as the acting team leader, would I be right in saying that you are involved in the strategy, the Prosecution strategy behind this case, and that is that you are intimately involved with the senior trial attorney in designing the investigation mission and the gathering of evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Now, I'd be very cautious in saying yes to that. As I mentioned before, the steering of the investigation in this particular case lay firmly at the feet of the trial attorney, namely Ekkehard Withopf, who was assigned to the case from his arrival at the Tribunal. Once the case -- once there is an indictment issued, clearly it becomes the role of the senior trial attorney to steer the Prosecution side of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would the senior trial attorney in this case have been involved also in the investigation stage leading to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Ekkehard Withopf was integrally involved right throughout his time here at the Tribunal, both as a trial attorney and then more recently upon his appointment as the senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But, of course, the senior trial attorney has had to work not only in this case but other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you yourself as the team leader, you mentioned that you supervised the other investigators and that you also coordinate the work of the analysts and the work of the language assistants.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I would suggest to you that amongst all the investigators in team number 9 the investigator that is closest to the Prosecution strategy would be you.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it that any proposal for an investigation mission following instructions by the senior trial attorney would first go to your desk before any one of your investigators would deploy to Central Bosnia to investigate part of this case.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's -- I can only answer that that would -- that wouldn't always be the case. I think it would be fair to say that on occasions if I am -- have some involvement in one of the other projects and can't be present when certain issues are discussed, then it would be other investigators dedicated to this project who would discuss strategy, objectives with either the senior trial attorney or others involved, other legal personnel involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yourself, Mr. Hackshaw, do you feel confident that you are aware of the challenges and the issues in this case?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, how many investigators can we find in team number 9?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Seven at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So seven investigators. And how many analysts and how many language assistants?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Three analysts at the present and four language assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we talk about an analyst, are these all members of what we call the military analysis team, or is it a mix from members of the military analysis team and also the leadership research team?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No. The three that are immediately attached to the team are criminal or intelligence analysts. The leadership research team and the military analytical team operate on a team basis, independently of us; however, we have assigned personnel from within those units who work specifically on our projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that's in addition to the persons we've mentioned, namely seven investigators, three analysts, four language assistants, yourself. That's the team.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can call upon dedicated persons from the leadership research team and from the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So those are the resources you have to work with in order to build up the cases for which you are responsible.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. That's the resources as they stand to date -- today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I -- you've been there for 18 months, but you were the leader. If I would ask you: How many missions have been conducted in this particular case in 18 months? I understand that you may not have the exact answer, but a rough figure.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: You're right, I don't have the exact figure. I would say probably between a dozen and two dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Between 12 and 24 missions --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- over the last 18 months.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, look, I would have to refer to other material to give you an accurate answer. I feel uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm more looking for averages so that we have an understanding of the situation in which you are placed to gather evidence in a case. Now, on the average, how many investigators would take part in investigating -- in an investigation mission? Is that investigators, analysts, language assistants, or how many people approximately on the average?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: It varies considerably. If it was a large mission the objective of which was to search a large archive, there could be a dozen personnel involved at the least. If it was simply interviewing a dozen crime-base witnesses, that could be done by two investigators over several weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that's -- a small mission or a typical witness-interviewing mission would consist of, on the average, two investigator and one language assistant, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No. It would normally consist of -- if it was two investigators doing witness interviewing, they would have two language assistants. They would be doing separate interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So a team approximately of four people. And those language assistants, are they always the ones that travel with you from the Tribunal or do you also use field language assistants that are provided to you from a field office, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: More often than not we use language assistants that are provided with us -- provided to us in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your mission base, if I can use this expression, in your case, working on Central Bosnia, would I be right in saying that your mission base would be Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because the Office of the Prosecution has an office in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct. And Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But for Central Bosnia, which one would you use? Or could you use both?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No. We would traditionally use the one in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you would in any investigation mission, you would fly to Sarajevo, and then I take it -- I suggest - I mean I'm not sure - that vehicles would be made available to you so that you could drive to Central Bosnia and perform your work.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one of the trials, of course, that you have been working on in 18 months is the trial against General Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this initially started in your knowledge, because you were -- I'm not sure if you were there when it began, but as a project in 1999.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct, and I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were there in 1999.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you were there to identify the initial in-house data leading to an approval to try and arrive with an investigation --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, with an indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Correct, yeah. Well, to start with, to identify information to get a investigation proposal approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you mentioned that as you get this investigation proposal approved it is very important for the team to establish some kind of a strategy in order as to what evidence it will go and obtain and where.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that such a proposal of course would be based on time, on money, on security, and, of course, most importantly, on the objective of what you're going to go and obtain.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, all those things. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that when you initially completed this project, that your target - correct me if that's a wrong terminology in your language. I just suggest that "target" is a word that you may have used - were crimes originally committed by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the crimes committed by the Mujahedin was an important aspect of your investigation.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as part the investigation proposal that was approved, finding out persons responsible for the crimes committed by the Mujahedin was one of your principal objectives. I can rephrase that if you want. Just -- I do not want to confuse you. I'm just suggesting to you that you made an investigation proposal. Is that -- that's correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, members of the team did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in that investigation proposal, you have targets or issues or -- what is the term that you do use?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: We would use -- "targets" is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: "Target" it will be. And one of those targets were crimes committed by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the taking of statements in the field, I would just like to come back very quickly to what my colleague -- the question that she asked you to see if I did understand correctly that a statement is first recorded in English, but on the basis of verbal answers given in Bosniak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. The investigator would either ask the witness questions or allow the witness to tell their story. Whatever questions or prompts the investigator would use would be then translated by a field interpreter into a language that's used by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: And then the answers or responses are then translated back into English. And they are what's recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then would I be correct in saying that the statement itself is not written on that occasion but that the normal practice is for the investigator and the language assistant to go back and to reflect over all the notes in order to draft up a statement? Is that the normal practice?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, that's not the normal practice at all. The normal practice is to record the statement in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is the statement drafted on the spot?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, the statement is typed up in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's typed up?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: It's typewritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct, in the majority of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in other cases, would it be -- would it happen that a statement would be typed up later when you come back either to The Hague or to Sarajevo and then you go back to see the witness and you show him the result and you ask him if he agrees with what has been typed up?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, I think -- that would be a very rare practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A rare practice.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Normally it's typed up with the witness being present.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if there are documents, of course, you've mentioned that usually they would be -- there were two types of documents, either the one that you take with yourself to the field and show to the witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's one type.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the one that the witness might give to you in the course of his interview.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that both documents would usually be attached to the statement.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: If the quantity is such that they can be easily annexed, then it makes good sense -- it's a good practice, I believe, to make sure that they're referred to in the body of the statement.
