utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, normally if you come back and this is, as you mentioned the procedure called is indexing information form, or the IF'ing.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that allows you to record this information into electronic form when you come back. So it's kind of scanned and put into a database.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yeah, the statement or material that's annexed to it or that accompanies it is -- first of all, it is referenced -- it's submitted to evidence along with the index information form, which is now called a mini information index form. That's simply -- I think the easiest way to describe it would be that it is a -- it's a cover page that allows us to electronically search for that reference material, whether it be a statement, video, document. It allows us to electronically search for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So normally it should be easy by entering the name of a witness to gather all the information that -- which was ever obtained by this witness.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, if we are talking about material that we have physically taken possession of ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if there's another team that saw the same witness and obtained a statement, would there be a way to cross-reference these two so that all statements could be disclosed to the Defence, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose in theory there is a way. When you prepare an indexing information form, it has the facility to electronically associate other material to it. For example, if I took a statement from a witness and they provided me with a substantial amount of documentation that perhaps was not necessarily related to the issue that I was talking about with them, obviously that information needs to be inputted into the system because although it might not be of interest to me it may well be of interest to another team. And we have the ability electronically to input material independently but associate it electronically. Now, I'm certainly not aware of it being a common practice for people to, say, for example, if a witness was interviewed in relation to the Blaskic trial in 1998 or 1999 and then that same witness is then re-interviewed by our team in the year 2000, it's -- as far as I'm aware, it's not a common practice to associate those two statements together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is not something that you would check for before you go.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Oh, certainly you would try and research anybody you were going to talk to before you went.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, but if there was -- you would not necessarily search for that material before you deployed to Central Bosnia, in the sense of getting their previous statement so that you can put everything together when you come back. That would not be common practice.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: You would try and research any previous statements, for obvious reasons. However, once you got back with a fresh statement, in many cases two or three years later from the same witness, you would not automatically associate them through the available electronic means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I fully understand. Now, a quick question: You mention that as part of your investigation duty, you said that you were to gather both information to prove but also to disprove the culpability of a target. Did I get this right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, absolutely right. It's -- you know, my understanding of evidence is that it's the facts, testimony, and documents which may be used to prove or disprove the matters under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you do get a document that tends to disprove, what -- are there any special procedures when you come back to put it in a separate pile and identify it immediately as Rule 68 material or -- how do you do that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Well, I think during the investigation phase, certainly before an indictment has been issued, there's an onus on people to at least be aware and to take into consideration other projects ongoing within the ICTY or within the Office of the Prosecution, because common sense is that one person's witness in this Tribunal may well be another person's target. So, yeah, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you do care about these things.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yeah, and more so as the information databases have become densely populated, this is more so -- this has become a more prominent feature. In fact, in mission planning now, it's generally expected that if I had a list of half a dozen witnesses that I intended to interview, then now it's a reasonably common practice to publish those potential witnesses to other team, because other teams, although they may have a different interest, they may still have an interest in a particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to more specific information on this particular case. I'd like to begin by confirming with you that you are aware that in the year 2000 a request for state assistance, or I think they are called RSAs, if I'm right.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: They're called -- anything, any request we make of another government is called an RFA, or a request for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A request for assistance, RFA.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you -- can you confirm that in 2002 three requests for assistance were forwarded - one to the Travnik cantonal prosecutor's office, one in the Travnik cantonal court, and one in the Zenica cantonal court, in order to obtain information as to criminal complaints or prosecutions or judgements of war crimes - whether any of those had been submitted or had arose from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: I'm -- yeah, I'm pretty sure that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I have these three letters here. These three letters are contested exhibits in this case. And just for the sake of the transcript, I would like to confirm that these requests, the one addressed to the Travnik cantonal prosecutor's office is contested exhibit 640; that the one addressed to the Zenica cantonal court is contested exhibit 638; and that the one addressed to the cantonal court in Travnik is contested exhibit 639. I'm not going to show you, because you're aware of these requests for assistance being forwarded to these three agencies to request if any war crimes had been prosecuted in those three agencies from the beginning of 1993 until somewhere in 1994, or the time period relevant to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that would make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in the three cases you did receive replies to your requests.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: I can only assume that you're correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that the three numbers that I have given are the replies that we have received, not the requests sent by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] The three numbers I just gave you, I see that the Prosecution on the other side -- the three contested exhibits I have are the replies that were received from these three agencies. Now, would I be correct in saying that on the basis of these replies you concluded as part of your investigation that General Hadzihasanovic had taken very limited measures to prevent war crimes or to punish the perpetrators of war crimes in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Sorry, without seeing the replies to refresh my memory, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd prefer -- maybe it's better if I do show you the documents so that there are no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the usher show the witness the three documents. I don't have copies, because these are documents that we all have in our possession. So could we have 638, 639, and 640. Mr. President, I have copies with me, so we can easily give them to the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the witness gets hold of the document, I think we need to verify the status of the document. Could we have a minute, please? [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's my understanding that my colleague who was with us before, Mr. Withopf, withdrew these documents. They were contested documents and they were documents that were withdrawn. Am I correct? I'm not sure if the Defence can assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are told that these documents were withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be some confusion, because you used the internal OTP number, but the contested documents have a different number. For example number 639 that you mentioned, this would be contested document 420; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are quite right. The three documents have the numbers which are the numbers from the first list. I would nevertheless like to show those three documents to the witness and then I will decide whether I wish to tender them myself or not. But I think it is important to show them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But let us check straight away whether those documents have been withdrawn or not. Madam Benjamin -- so it's not 638, 639, 640 but 420, 419 and probably 418. So 418, 419, 420. Have they been withdrawn? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, there was a confusion with the numbers. They have not been withdrawn. They are 418, 419 and 420. Thanks. So my friend confused us a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Luckily, the Judges know the documents by heart. So let us show the documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I also wish to thank the Chamber for identifying the documents. I just checked whether the expert used these documents, and he did, but I didn't verify the numbers, so I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Hackshaw, I would simply ask that you take a quick look at those documents. See if you recall ever seeing those replies from those three organisations giving you information as to what if any war crimes had been either purported, prosecuted, or on which there may have been a ruling --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- in the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen these before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hackshaw, can you confirm that on the basis of these documents, that it was your assessment -- and when I say "your," I'm talk about team 9's assessment, of course -- that General Hadzihasanovic had taken very limited measures to prevent or punish war crimes during the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I beg to object. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think this is for this witness to decide. I really don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are asking a legal question which has repercussions on the criminal responsibility of the accused and it is not up to the witness to respond to such a question, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. All that I was asking was to ask the investigator - he has instructions, he needs to find documents, discuss them with others - and then the prosecutors enter into the game. But as an professional investigator, he could have an opinion. I could ask him his opinion as a professional investigator working in the OTP whether his conclusion was, on the basis of these documents, that very little measures were taken -- very few measures were taken by General Hadzihasanovic either to prevent or to punish war crimes. I think that this question can be put to such a witness. But I am in your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have heard the question, which is a relevant question you're being asked. But let us not forget after all that you were the head of team 9. You were a high-level investigator, therefore. And a high-level investigator is capable, on the basis of documents, not to make a legal analysis, but to have a basis on which to think over the direction his investigations will take. So the question that is being put to you: Having read these three responses coming from a judicial authority, can you answer the question that has been put to you by the Defence? In your capacity as investigator, not as your -- not as a Prosecutor, because that is not your role, but documents that you have in front of you, do they allow you at your level - not at the level of the supreme responsibility of the Prosecutor - to draw any conclusions? So can you answer this question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can. Yes, I think I can, in part. I think in relation to 638, that lists nine people's names, I would say that would cause me to want to explore the issues further. I think in relation to 639, which discusses the Travnik district military court, that would also cause me to want to explore the issue of referrals through the district military prosecutor further. And the third one, 640, I think -- yeah, that would at the very least make me want to explore the issues of referrals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hackshaw. I'll take these documents back, as they are contested exhibits, and I'll -- I do not have intention to withdraw the objection of the Defence, but I thought it was important for you to recognise them so we are at least one step closer to, of course, these documents being admissible. Now, Mr. Hackshaw, on the basis of your answer you just gave me, can you confirm that these three documents -- of course, they were received. You saw the dates in April of 2002 and May of 2002. Did you have a chance to see those dates?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll just say that 640 -- no, the right numbers are -- so the exact numbers is the document from the cantonal prosecutor's office in Travnik is dated 16th of April, 2002; and that the document from the cantonal court in Travnik is dated 22nd of April, 2002; and the document from the Zenica cantonal court is dated the 10th of May, 2002. Now, Mr. Hackshaw, you can confirm that all these three documents, these replies, were received well after the filing of the indictment against General Hadzihasanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if I look at the reference, in terms of when these requests were sent to those three agencies - I'm not going to go through the dates - but you wouldn't be surprised in learning that they were also sent to these three agencies way after the initial appearance of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that on the reception of this letter this was an element of information that would tend to show that the indictment was correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: I think it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It went -- in the sense of your investigation.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, would you also -- would you confirm to me that having received this information, you did not -- or no actual teams, no investigation mission were sent to look at the archives of the Zenica cantonal court, of the Travnik cantonal court, and of the Travnik cantonal public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, not immediately after. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not until your mission in June of 2004.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No. There were some previous to that. I think at the latter part of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of -- we've talked about the replies. Now, today, as the team leader of -- of team number 9, you now know that the situation is completely different. Are you aware?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, sorry, I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will rephrase this question. You had a picture that you made some conclusions on the basis of these three replies that you received in 2002. I guess we agree on this.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No. I think -- well, the conclusion that I draw if those looking at them today is that certain aspects certainly needed to be explored further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And -- but you now know -- I put it to you that you know on the basis of the evidence that has been introduced in evidence in this case that the picture is very different from what you could get from these three letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I wouldn't allow the witness to answer that. Mr. President, I have to object. This witness is not in conduct of this trial. My friend has been trying that since with the last witness. This witness is not in conduct of this trial. This is an investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm afraid you're going too far. The question you are putting to the witness is absolutely the responsibility of the Prosecution. The investigator as such has not been conducting the Prosecution from A to Z. So your question is going outside what the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But I have shown him the documents that are in the file, and I'm asking him to make conclusions as an investigator, to compare two documents that he obtained during the investigation. I would like to ask the registrar if he could show the witness again documents DH274, a document admitted today; another one, DH119, dated the 10th of January, 1994; and another document, DH155, a document dated the 20th of March, 1994. We have given the registrar a list with the numbers, so I don't think it will take too long and he will quickly be able to find those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to apologise to the Chamber. We wanted to save the Chamber of too many binders, but tomorrow we will photocopy the documents and prepare a binder for you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you sure of your numbers, DH119 and 155?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Hackshaw, I would like you to take a quick look and that you would begin with the document which bears the number DH155, and that is a document which is dated on the 20th of March, 1994. Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that this is a document that comes from the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps and that is addressed to the security sector of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that according to this report you can see that "In the period" - and I quote from paragraph A - where it says that "In the period of 14th September 1992 to 1 March of 1994 a total of 377 criminal reports were filed," and then you have a breakdown of these reports. And if you follow with me, would you agree that there are members of the BH army, 17 officers and 295 soldiers; and that the HVO, 7 officers and 206 soldiers; civilians, 274; and then Ministry of the Interior, 1; and then Serb soldiers, 4; and not found or at least not identified, 20? Is this what this document is saying?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm simply asking you, Mr. Hackshaw, whether this document, as the leader of team number 9, was shown to you when it was introduced in evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is the information contained in this document something that was shown to you -- in the sense of look at all these criminal reports -- is that something that was shown to you or discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: I believe that I'm familiar -- I've seen either this or a similar document. It may not necessarily be for that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But this was actually introduced in evidence in the first week of May. Can you confirm that between the first week of May and now this is information that you had to discuss as your duty, as the leader of team number 9?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No, I haven't discussed this with the Prosecution team that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next document, and that is a document DH119, dated 10 January 1994. Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at this document, I look at -- this is a document that comes from a report on the work of the Travnik disciplinary military prosecutor's office for the year 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this document -- is this document or the contents thereof something that was discussed with you from -- between the month of May and now, in terms of your investigation into this case?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: From May this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May of this year?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: To now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Until today.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Not that I recall specifically, no. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move to the third document, and this is a document which is DH274. Do you have this document with you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: No. I have something that has "234" handwritten on it. That's probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's a document dated 12 December 1993.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You have it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, you this document comes from the Zenica direct military court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would refer to the fourth paragraph, beginning with the word "during." Do you see this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I simply quote the paragraph: "During this year, the court received a total of 432 criminal charges involving 869 individuals, out of which number 250 cases involving 573 individuals were completed and 182 cases involving 236 individuals are still in progress."

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I'd agree that's what's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is this a document or the information contained in this document something that was discussed with you as the leader of team number 9 between the first week of May when it was introduced and today?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Not that I have any recall. Not personally with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I ask you, Mr. Hackshaw, whether between the first week of May and now there was a change in your investigation due to the fact that there was much evidence introduced into this trial which shows that General Hadzihasanovic has taken numerous steps?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, no, no, Mr. President. No. That is out of order. This witness is not involved in this trial. He's not presumed to know the evidence that has been led in this trial, and he's asking him to speculate, and I would not -- I have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The question put to you appears to assume that you were informed of all the documents admitted into evidence. So Ms. Benjamin is explaining that the witness is not in charge of the trial. The only question you can put to him is that when he went on mission sometime ago, was he familiar with these documents. And he said no. So I think he said all that can be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let me rephrase the question in a different way which will allow the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] Can you confirm as a leader of team number 9 that over the recent months there has been a focus in the investigation that you are leading because of the evidence introduced in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But that is precisely the same way that you put it just now in another way. He does not have any control over the evidence that is being led in this case and how the evidence is led. This is an investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is repeating that this witness is only an investigator but still a high-level investigator. But he's not in charge of the Prosecution, so it is Ms. Benjamin that could have asked the question and not you. So he can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But to finish off for today, I would liking to ask the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] You were asked to go on a mission in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is the mission that you described earlier on to my colleague when she put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you described the aim of that mission, which was to visit first the Zenica high public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: The mission was to visit the prosecution service in Zenica and in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two places.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you decided -- when this specific investigation mission was approved, what was the basis for taking on this mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: My understanding of the basis that over recent months there had been attempts by the investigation and Prosecution team to try and clarify the issues surrounding referrals, who referrals were made through of allegations of criminal misconduct. And as such, the team had established that the correct procedure was that every referral in relation to military personnel should have gone through the district military prosecutor. And my objective was to see what material had in fact gone through the relevant district military prosecutor during the time of our indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hackshaw. I have one last question which I will put to you with a document, and I will -- I guess this will be all we have time for today. Now, this is a letter which was addressed to both Defence teams by the Prosecution concerning your mission in Central Bosnia. And I would like you to take a look at this letter and I will put some questions to you on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a letter that we received from the Prosecution. I've already told my learned friend that I intend to use this letter during the cross-examination, and I have copies for all the parties in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Hackshaw, having seen this letter, have you seen this letter before?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I think I have, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer you to the second paragraph. First let me ask you: You confirm that this, of course, has a direct link with your mission in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I refer you to the second paragraph, which says that "The task of the Prosecution is currently undertaking in this respect..." Now, this task, would I be correct in saying that this task is to identify cases handled by the legal system in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Handled or referred through the district military prosecutor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: "And that this task was complicated by the fact that the perpetrators of such offences are generally unknown." This is what this letter says.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: That's what the letter says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that -- if I go on with this paragraph, that it says that "To this end, the Prosecution is looking for the help of the defence in identifying who the perpetrators are." Is that about what this letter says?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW
utterances.text: Well, yes, they're asking for your knowledge of any specific cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my last question for today, Mr. President. Tomorrow things may be corrected, but I believe that I have used an hour today which means that tomorrow I am still left with a half an hour, with your permission, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Since we have only this witness tomorrow, we will have lots of time at our disposal. I believe that you will be given your 30 minutes and the other Defence team is going to have some time for their possible questions, and Mrs. Benjamin will probably have some questions in re-examination, and the Judges will need at least one hour. So yes, you will be given the floor tomorrow to resume your cross-examination. Mr. Witness, you have entered into solemn declaration. You are a witness to the justice. Your situation is the same as of any other witness, which means from today to tomorrow you are not supposed to talk to anybody, not even to your superior, because your testimony will continue tomorrow. Once you leave the courtroom, you have to go straight home. You are not supposed to meet with your superiors, and you will please come back tomorrow at 9.00. And once your testimony is finished, you will be able to talk to everybody, but from today to tomorrow you are not supposed to talk to anybody because this rule applies to all the witnesses. This is an fortunate situation because you are coming back tomorrow. If we were to tell you to come back in six months, then you would not be able to talk to your superiors for six months. Again, I would like to invite all of you to come back tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened only Tuesday, the 29th day of June, 2004 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
